claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a simple, disordered solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution is likely BCC.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has relatively low hardness and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable ductility and machinability.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has minimal lattice distortion.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has minimal secondary-phase or nanoscale-precipitate formation.
Minimal lattice distortion and the absence of nanoscale precipitates cause the low hardness and strength of the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Minimal lattice distortion and absent precipitates permit relatively unimpeded dislocation glide.
Plastic deformation in the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is grain-boundary-mediated.
Al has a sufficiently different atomic radius from the CoCrFeNiTi constituents to increase atomic-size mismatch.
Adding approximately 3–5 at.% Al to CoCrFeNiTi will increase local lattice distortion.
Adding approximately 3–5 at.% Al may nucleate nanoscale precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Enhanced local lattice strain impedes dislocation glide.
Fine precipitates impede dislocation glide and increase yield strength.
A 3–5 at.% Al addition will produce measurably higher hardness and yield strength than baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
Microstructural strengthening can increase strength without completely eliminating ductility.
The Al-modified alloy may have lower ductility than baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
The solute addition will shift deformation from grain-boundary-mediated plasticity toward a more dislocation-controlled, pinning-dominated regime.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as undergoing both unimpeded dislocation glide and grain-boundary-mediated plasticity, while the modified state is predicted to become more dislocation-controlled despite adding barriers to dislocation motion. The intended distinction between the baseline and modified deformation regimes is therefore mechanistically ambiguous.

The prediction requires only a measurable increase in hardness and yield strength, whereas the falsification rule requires greater than 10% improvement. A statistically significant increase below 10% could satisfy the stated prediction but still be classified as falsification.
